title: Two machines, six print jobs
intro: Quick Print has two identical machines, M1 and M2, both free at minute 0. Six jobs, J1 to J6, wait in a queue in that order. A machine does one job at a time, without a break.
clues: Jobs are taken from the queue one at a time, in queue order.
Each job goes to whichever machine becomes free first and starts at once; if both machines are free at the same moment, M1 is used.
A job's waiting time is the time from minute 0 until it starts.

questions.stem: At what minute (counting from minute 0) does the last of the six jobs finish, if the jobs are taken in the order J1, J2, J3, J4, J5, J6?
why: J1 to M1 (0 to 40), J2 to M2 (0 to 25), J3 to M2 (25 to 60), J4 to M1 (40 to 60).
Both machines are free at 60: J5 to M1 (60 to 90), J6 to M2 (60 to 75). The last job ends at minute 90.

questions.stem: In the order J1 to J6, on which machine does J5 run, and when?
why: When J5 is taken, both machines become free at minute 60 (M1 after J4, M2 after J3).
At a tie M1 is used: J5 runs on M1 from minute 60 to minute 90.

questions.stem: What is the total waiting time, in minutes, of the six jobs when they are taken in the order J1 to J6?
why: The start times are J1 0, J2 0, J3 25, J4 40, J5 60 and J6 60.

questions.stem: The owner changes the queue order to shortest job first, using the same rule. By how many minutes does the total waiting time fall?
why: Order J6, J4, J2, J5, J3, J1: J6 M1 0 to 15, J4 M2 0 to 20, J2 M1 15 to 40, J5 M2 20 to 50, J3 M1 40 to 75, J1 M2 50 to 90.

questions.stem: If the owner can choose any order of the six jobs (still using the same rule), what is the earliest minute at which all six jobs can be finished?
why: The jobs need 165 minutes in all, so one machine works at least 82.5 minutes. Every job is a multiple of 5 minutes, so the finish is at least 85.
Order J1, J3, J5, J2, J4, J6 reaches it: M1 runs J1, J2, J4 (40 + 25 + 20 = 85), M2 runs J3, J5, J6 (35 + 30 + 15 = 80).

steps: Keep a "free at" time for each machine. Give each job, in queue order, to the machine free first (M1 at a tie); it starts then and the machine is free again after the job's minutes.
J1 and J2 start at 0. M2 is free first (25) for J3; M1 at 40 for J4; both at 60, so J5 goes to M1 and J6 to M2. M1 finishes at 90, M2 at 75.

Waiting time is the start time, so the total is the sum of starts. For the best possible finish, divide the total work by two machines and round up to the time unit, then find an order that reaches it.

diagram.note: Minutes from 0 along the bottom; each bar is a job on its machine.

title: A renovation with nine tasks
intro: A renovation has nine tasks, A to I. The table gives the days each task needs and the tasks it must wait for.
clues: Each task needs one whole crew for its full duration and cannot be paused once started.
A task can start only after every task it must wait for has finished; a task with no restriction can start at day 0.
Unless a question says otherwise, there are as many crews as needed, so tasks that are allowed to run together do.

questions.stem: What is the least number of days in which the whole renovation can be completed?
why: A (3) + B (4) + C (3) finish C at day 10; E ends at 13, and F and H at 18.
D ends at 12, G at 16 and I at 4, so the last task finishes at day 18.

questions.stem: Which one of the following single delays, each considered on its own, would make the whole renovation finish later than the least possible time?
options: F takes 1 day longer than planned
D takes 5 days longer than planned
G takes 2 days longer than planned
I takes 10 days longer than planned
why: F is on the longest chain (A, B, C, E, F), which has no spare time, so any delay to F delays the end.
G has 2 days to spare, D 6 and I 14, so their delays are absorbed.

questions.stem: Task E is speeded up so that it takes only 1 day instead of 3 (everything else unchanged). What is the new least number of days for the whole renovation?
why: E now ends at day 11, so F and H end at 16.
G also ends at 16 (C ends at 10, then 6 days). The renovation ends at day 16.

questions.stem: There are only two crews, and every task needs one whole crew (a task is never shared between crews). A crew may wait between tasks. What is the least number of days in which all nine tasks can be completed?
why: A, B and C run one after another, so C cannot end before day 10, and D, E, F, G and H all wait for it. Those five need 21 crew-days; two crews need at least 10.5 days, so at least 11 in whole tasks: day 21 at the earliest.
It can be done: crew 1 does A, B, C, E, F, D (ending at 20); crew 2 does I (0 to 4), G (10 to 16) and H (16 to 21).

fig.note: Days along the bottom; each bar is a task done by that crew.

questions.stem: With two crews as in the previous question, task C is now shortened to 2 days (everything else unchanged). What is the least number of days for all nine tasks?
why: C can now end at day 9, and the 21 crew-days of D, E, F, G and H still need at least 11 days on two crews: day 20 at the earliest.
Crew 1: A, B, C, E, F, D (ending at 19); crew 2: I (0 to 4), G (9 to 15), H (15 to 20). So 20 days.

steps: Draw each task with its days and an arrow from every task it waits for. I waits for nothing and nothing waits for it.
Forward pass: a task starts when the last task it waits for ends. A 0 to 3, B 3 to 7, C 7 to 10, then D 10 to 12, E 10 to 13, G 10 to 16, F and H 13 to 18, and I 0 to 4. The project ends at day 18.

Backward pass: a task's spare time is how much later it could end without moving day 18. A, B, C, E, F and H have none (the critical path); G has 2, D 6, I 14. With limited crews, find the stage that holds the rest back (C) and divide the work left after it by the crews.

diagram.note: Each task shows its days, then the days it runs; the bold arrows are the critical path.

title: Timetabling eight exams
intro: A university must schedule eight exam papers, A to H, into time slots. A slot can hold as many papers as the rooms allow; the limit is stated in each question.
clues: Two papers clash if at least one student takes both, and clashing papers cannot be in the same slot.
The clashes are exactly these twelve pairs, and no others: A-C, A-D, A-E, A-F, B-D, C-G, C-H, D-E, D-G, E-F, E-G, F-H.
A paper is never split across slots.

questions.stem: If there is no limit on the number of papers in a slot, what is the smallest number of slots in which all eight papers can be held without a clash?
why: A, D and E clash with each other in every pair, so they need three different slots.
Three are enough: A, B, G | C, D, F | E, H has no clash inside any slot.

questions.stem: The exams are on three days, Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday, with at most 3 papers on any day. In how many different ways can the eight papers be assigned to the three days, if it matters which group is on which day?
why: There are exactly 4 ways to split the papers into three groups of at most 3 (see the walkthrough): A, B, G | C, D, F | E, H; A, G, H | B, C, E | D, F; A, G, H | B, E | C, D, F; and A, G | B, E, H | C, D, F.
Each split's three groups can go to the three days in 3 x 2 x 1 = 6 ways: 4 x 6 = 24.

questions.stem: With three slots and at most 3 papers in a slot, which pair of papers must be in the same slot in every valid timetable?
why: In all four splits A and G are together (and so are D and F).
B and E are apart in A, B, G | C, D, F | E, H; E and H, and C and F, are apart in A, G, H | B, C, E | D, F.

questions.stem: There are now four slots, but the rooms are smaller: exactly 2 papers fit in a slot, so each slot gets exactly 2 papers. In how many ways can the eight papers be split into four pairs with no clash inside any pair? (The order of the slots does not matter.)
why: List each paper's possible partners (those it does not clash with) and go through A's partner. A with B gives 3 ways, A with G gives 5, A with H gives 2.

questions.stem: In the setting of the previous question (four slots, exactly two papers each), two more clashes are discovered: B-F and B-H. In how many ways can the papers now be split into four pairs with no clash inside any pair?
why: Of the ten splits, three pair B with F or with H: A-G, D-C, B-F, E-H; A-G, D-F, B-H, C-E; and A-G, D-H, B-F, C-E.
The other 7 remain.

steps: Draw the papers as dots and each clash as a line. Papers joined by a line need different slots.
A, D and E clash pairwise (a triangle), so with three slots they take one slot each: call them slot 1, 2 and 3. Every other paper joins one of these.
Place the rest by their clashes. F clashes with A and E, so it joins D in slot 2; G clashes with D and E, so it joins A in slot 1. C can go in slot 2 or 3, H in slot 1 or 3, and B in slot 1 or 3.

With at most 3 papers a slot: C in slot 2 fills it (C, D, F), and B and H share out slots 1 and 3 in three ways; C in slot 3 leaves one place each in slots 1 and 3, and only H in slot 1, B in slot 3 avoids the C-H clash. That is 4 splits in all.

diagram.note: A line joins two papers that clash; the bold triangle A, D, E needs three slots.
